exchange.text: "Futures." She taps the table with the chrome finger. "Sealed sheets: a place, a date, a thing that happens. Somebody knows. No, I won't say who, at this table, for free."

map.text: She puts the glasses on and does not touch the cloth. For a long time she reads the blocks beside the pins the way other people read faces. "Oh, my dear." Very quietly. "That's ours. That's the Exchange's hand — the notation, I mean; I taught it to the girl who taught it to the clerks. Twelve lots." She takes the glasses off. "I can read every one of these. Two a night; more and the eyes go, and the eyes are the only thing I have that isn't borrowed."

price.text: "A seat at your fire, east. And when we reach the place that holds my trade, one hour of your time and no questions until it's done." She holds out the chrome hand. "That is the whole contract. I've written longer ones for less."

packet.text: She weighs the packet in the chrome hand without touching the seal, turns it to the lamp, and sniffs the wax. "Water." She hands it back. "That's a schedule. Somebody here buys a town's water by the measure, in advance." She looks at your Sallow boots. "Yours, I expect. Deliver it or don't. Opening it costs more than you have."

text.text: "The floor. The protection account, out of the Sarr ledger, by the floor's order — two riders, four days, *westbound traveller, confirmed*. I'd swear to it, and I've read the line." odroom_stand.again: The lamp back on its hook. NB-1 in its frame.

odroom_trust.speaker: narrator
odroom_trust.text: She looks at you for a moment as if you had paid her in a coin she did not recognise. Then she hangs the lamp back on its hook. "Nobody has ever let me choose a thing I was owed a say in. I'd forgotten how heavy it is." NB-1 stays in its frame. Her sheet goes inside her coat.
odroom_trust.again: The lamp on its hook, unlit. NB-1 where it was.

odroom_first.speaker: narrator
odroom_first.text: She takes NB-1 out of its frame, glass and tin and a sheet no bigger than a hand, folds it once, and feeds it to the lamp's chimney. It goes brown, and then it goes. Only that one. "That one was mine," she says. "The rest belong to the people on them." She hangs the lamp up. Her own sheet goes inside her coat.
odroom_first.again: An empty frame by the door. The rest in their rows.

odroom_no.speaker: narrator
odroom_no.text: "No." She does not raise her voice; she puts her hand, the one that is hers, flat over the lamp's hook. "Not with my hand, my dear. Every sheet in here is somebody sold, yes. Every sheet in here also says who bought them. Burn the room and the buyers were never here." She does not move her hand.
odroom_no.again: Her hand flat over the lamp's hook. She has not moved it.

decision.text: Odile took her sheet on Shale out of the paper room at Ninebridge and left the room standing.

odroom_left.speaker: narrator
odroom_left.text: "You asked. That is a cost; I'll carry it." She takes her hand off the hook. Her sheet goes inside her coat, and she walks out of the room ahead of you and does not look at the rows again.
odroom_left.again: The rows, standing. Odile already outside.

odroom_burned.speaker: narrator
odroom_burned.text: Lamp oil on dry paper goes the way the Sallow goes in a dry year, all at once and then row by row, by place, by date. Odile stands in the doorway with her sheet in the chrome hand and watches the whole road burn, and does not try to stop you again. When the roof of the container begins to tick with the heat she says, "That was a cost," quite pleasantly, and walks down the deck toward the Span without looking back to see whether you follow.
odroom_burned.again: Smoke out of the welded seams, and the smell of wax.

decision.text: You burned the paper room behind the Grand Factor's office at Ninebridge, every sheet in it. Odile walked back to the Span without you.

news.text: the paper room behind the Grand Factor's office burned with every sheet in it, and the floor sold nothing for a week

contract.text: "The floor pays ninety for lot four. The clerk handles it; I don't touch paper that small." She goes back to the pen. "Unless you were going to ask me to tear it up, in which case: not at that price."

fight.text: She has not moved from the desk. "You'll find the guild is credit, and I am the guild. Go on, then."
fight.again: She has still not moved from the desk. The clocks go on.

intro.text: The captain of the deck guard stands mid-span where he can see both ramps and the planks, and does not stop seeing them to talk to you. "Dent. Weapons stay down on the deck. Trouble goes in the river. The ninth span fell on its own; everything since, somebody pushed."

options.text: The block on the east bank.
Why hasn't the guild mended the span?

again.text: "Captain." His eyes are on the ramps.
again.again: He watches a porter cross the deck, and waits.

strike.text: "Voss is a decent man with ruined knees and the guild will starve him anyway, because it has paper that says it can." He does not lower his voice. "I keep the deck. I don't keep the ramp. That's Bors's, and I thank the river for it."

block.text: "Fen sells debt. Somebody has to; the guild is credit and credit has to go somewhere when it goes bad." He watches a porter not carrying. "He hates it, which is why he's good at it. The ones who like it get careless."

span.text: "Two Tolls of planks against twelve a head to cross one at a time, slow, in sight of the guard." He almost smiles. "The guild doesn't mend things that pay better broken."

fight.again: The captain has the deck guard between you and the ramps. Nobody is talking.

text.text: TODAY'S LOTS, in chalk. Lot four has a line through it.
TODAY'S LOTS, in chalk. 1 — PORTER, 40, SUM 31. 2 — COOK, 55, SUM 19. 3 — CLERK, 23, SUM 70. 4 — CALLOWAY, S., 19, SUM 58 AND INTEREST. 5 — MECHANIC, 48, SUM 44. Under the fourth, smaller: OPENS 60.

passives.text: Calloway. Wren's name. The Sallow is not so large that it is a common one.

intro.text: The auctioneer is young for the voice: a bright, carrying, cheerful voice that does not reach his eyes. "Lots at nine, settled by six, no credit, the guild is credit. Lot four's young, if that's what you came for. Everyone's come for lot four today. I open at sixty."

passives.text: His hands are shaking very slightly, and he keeps them on the counter so they don't show. He has looked at the cage exactly once.

options.text: (Let it go. Someone else will buy her.)

text.text: "Lot four's off the board." The voice, cheerful. The hands, on the counter. "Lot five, a mechanic."
"Lot four. Sixty opens it."

again.again: He says a sum to the crowd and waits for you between lots.

lot7.text: "Lot seven. Bexley, forty-one, a mechanic, forty-eight and interest. Signed for parts he fitted to a truck that then left without him." The voice, and under it: "Nobody comes for mechanics. He's been on the board since spring." He looks at you properly for the first time. "Seventy opens it. There is nobody to bid against you. There never is."

options.text: Nobody's bidding. Fifty, and your board is a card shorter.

lot7_low.text: "Fifty." He writes it in the voice that says sums. "Going — gone, to the stranger at fifty, and the guild can take the twenty out of my cheer." The paper comes across.

lot7_firm.text: "Seventy opens it. The guild counts what I open at, not what I close at."

lot7_sold.text: "Lot seven." The thumb-print on the paper is a working man's, broad and oil-dark. "He's wherever the guild has him working till the paper says otherwise. Whoever you're buying for — " He stops himself. "I say the sums."

four.text: "Sable Calloway, nineteen, fifty-eight and interest. Her brother's debt, if you want the story — he signed and ran, and the paper doesn't care who signed." The voice does not change. "Service until cleared. Most buyers want a cook or a carrier. Some want nineteen." He looks at the counter. "I say the sums. I don't say the rest."

interject.text: "The girl," Wren says, so low it is nearly nothing. Then her face shuts like a door and she is a scout again, counting the guards round the cage.

bid.text: "Sixty from the stranger." The voice rises and the crowd leans. "Seventy from the back. Eighty — the gentleman in the coat, thank you, eighty." He looks at you. He is very slightly, under the voice, on your side.

options.text: (Talk the room down.) The coat bought lot two for a cook. He doesn't want a girl, he wants to be seen.

bid_low.text: The coat colours, and finds he has business elsewhere, and the back goes quiet. "Seventy, then. Going — gone, to the stranger at seventy." The hammer is a tin cup on the counter.

bid_high.text: "Ninety from the coat." He will not look at you. "Against you, stranger."

sold.text: "Sold." The contract comes across the counter with a thumb-print already on it that is not yours. "She's yours till it clears. The cage key's on the paper. I don't ask what for." Very quietly, under the voice: "Please don't make me wish I had."

hate_ok.text: The voice stops. What is left is a man of thirty with shaking hands. "Every day. Every lot." He looks at the cage, the second time. "I can't lose a lot in daylight; the guild counts. But the box isn't counted till nine, and I lock it badly, and I sleep by the fire on the east bank." He does not say anything else. He does not need to.

hate_no.text: The voice does not even flicker. "Everybody hates it, friend. I'm paid to say the sums." He turns to the crowd. "Lot four, sixty, do I hear sixty."

night_help.text: He is by the fire on the east bank, awake, not looking at the block. "Box is open. Paper's on top. The cage key's under it." He looks into the fire. "If anyone asks, you stole it, and I'll say so with my whole chest."
night_help.again: Still by the fire, still not looking at the block. "It's still open," he says.

took.text: "Lot four, stolen in the night," he says to the fire, in the voice, and then not in it: "Thank you."

let_go.text: "Lot four, sixty — seventy — ninety to the gentleman in the coat, going, gone." The cup on the counter. The crowd moves to lot five. Somebody opens the cage.

interject.text: Wren watches the coat go with the paper in his pocket. She does not say anything. She does not look at you, then or for a long time after.
Odile watches the coat take the paper, and you can see her price it, and see her hate that she did.
Ash looks at the cage a long time after it is empty.
Ilya counts the cup coming down on the counter. "Right," he says, and nothing else.

off.text: Off the block he is somebody else: smaller, by the fire, with a cup. "Lots at nine. I don't sell at night; it's the one rule I made myself."
off.again: He lifts the cup an inch by way of a greeting. "Nine," he says. "Not before."

text.text: "Lot four, stolen, lost, mislaid — I've said all three to the guild and they wrote down the one they liked." He almost smiles. "Lot seven's a mechanic. Nobody comes for mechanics."
"Lot eight. A carrier, thirty." The voice is back, and the board is one card shorter.
"Lot seven. A mechanic, forty-eight." The voice is back.

intro.text: A young woman on a cot in a cage, knees up, who looks at you the way the lots look at the crowd: as a sum. "Sixty. I heard him. If you've sixty, don't stand there being sorry about it."

passives.text: A burn scar on the inside of her left forearm, old, the shape of a hand that grabbed. Wren has one like it, on her left hand.

options.text: You've a sister. A scout, with the Dogs.

again.again: She has her chin on her knees again. "Sixty," she says, to the bars.

name.text: "Sable. Calloway, if the paper wants it. My brother signed for a bike and rode it away and the paper doesn't care who signed." She looks at the chalk board. "I had a sister. Everyone had a sister once."

wren.text: Wren has not said a word since the block came in sight. Now she steps up to the cage and says, "Sable," and the girl on the cot looks up and says nothing at all for a long time, and then, "You left," and Wren says, "I know," and that is all either of them can manage.

sister.text: Something goes across her face and is put away. "Wren." Not a question. "Is she alive?" You tell her. "Then she can come and buy me herself." But she has turned so you cannot see her eyes.

text.text: You hold her paper. Wren is looking at you, not at her sister.
You hold her paper. She has seen the thumb-print on it and has stopped looking at you as a sum and started looking at you as weather.

options.text: (Give her the contract.) It's yours. Tear it.

decision.text: You put Sable Calloway's debt contract in her own hands at the Ninebridge block.

options.text: (Keep it.) You work for me until it clears.

freed.text: She tears it in half and in half again, slowly, as if it might be a trick, and then she is standing outside the cage with four pieces of paper in her fist and nowhere to put them. "I'm going west," she says. "To Shale. There was a sister." She does not thank you; she has decided not to. Then, at the ramp, she does, without turning round.

interject.text: Wren watches her all the way to the ramp. "Four pieces," she says at last, to nobody. "She always tore things in four."
"Paper is only paper," Odile says softly, "until somebody tears it." She looks pleased, and tries not to.
"Good," Ash says, the way he says it to a row that came up.

kept.text: She stands up off the cot and folds the blanket and does not look at you. "Where do you sleep? I'll keep it." Her voice is level. Wren, if she is here, has walked away down the deck and will not be found until morning.

interject.text: "You bought a person," Tamsin says. It isn't a question, and she doesn't wait for an answer; she walks off after Wren.
"Right," Ilya says, and that is all he says for the rest of the day.
"You bought a person, friend," Ash says. "Hold the paper, then. Feel what it weighs."

intro.text: "Guns, cells, and things that were somebody's." A broad woman behind a counter of oiled steel, a machine pistol slung and a boxed something under the counter she does not mention. "Guild price on the sign; your price on your face."
intro.again: Oyo looks you over again and revises the price on your face. "Well?"

chrome.text: "Chrome. Concern-made, sealed, a leg that doesn't tire. I don't fit it; the Sink has people for that, or the Mender in Shale if you're going back." She does not open the box. "Ask when you've the coin. Everyone asks before."

intro.text: "Water, jerky, tins. Fruit from Openfield when the Choir sends it, and they haven't — blight, they say, or the guild says it for them." An old man with a goatee and a tin cup. "Eat something. You look like a forecast."
intro.again: "Still no fruit." Gunnar rattles the tin cup. "Still tins."

look.text: Guild paper, wax, the half-moon. On the outside: LOT 3 — NINEBRIDGE — DAY 2. Odile said the seal is the product. Opened, it is only news.
look.again: LOT 3 — NINEBRIDGE — DAY 2, under the half-moon, unbroken.

read.text: NINEBRIDGE — PORTERS' STOPPAGE — ENDS THIRD DAY, STRAPS ON, TERMS UNCHANGED. Dated the day before the porters sat down. The hand is not the clerk's; it is nobody's — too even, every letter the same.

sealed.text: Oilcloth, wax, the guild's half-moon. Lighter than it should be. The clerk at Tollhouse 9 said: opened, the bearer owes a sum nobody has.
sealed.again: The packet, sealed. Still lighter than it should be.

decision.text: You broke the seal on the guild's packet and read it.

opened.text: One sheet. SHALE — WATER — 0.62 — and a date a month after you stood at Dry Wells, and a sum, and no signature, in a hand too even to be a hand. A schedule for a town's thirst, sold in advance to whoever wanted to know.
opened.again: SHALE — WATER — 0.62, in a hand too even to be a hand.

day.text: The well: a wheel on a timber frame over a shaft, a pipe to two stone troughs, north and south. The north trough feeds the field rows; the south, the halls. Moss on the south trough. The north one is clean as a plate.
day.again: The wheel, the two troughs: moss on the south, the north scoured clean.

passives.text: Clean because it is scoured — nothing grows in it. There is a bitter smell off the north water that the south water does not have.

mods.why: you know which trough to test

options.text: (Read the ground round the north trough.)

test_ok.text: Iodine from the healer's shelf, a tin cup, patience. The south trough stays brown. The north goes the grey-green of a thing that should not be drunk: a metal salt, dosed, not leached. The glass did not do this. Someone did, at the north trough, at night.

test_no.text: Both troughs taste of stone. Without a reagent you cannot say more than the Elder says: something is wrong with the water and the rows.

tracks_ok.text: One set of boots comes to the north trough every night — the dust is beaten flat in a line nobody else walks — and goes back west, not to the halls but to the small hut past the seed store. A man's boots, heavy on the left. The Elder's son walks like that.

tracks_no.text: Forty people drink here. The ground is a page everyone has written on.

night.text: The well in the dark. The windpump creaks over the burial ground; the halls are shut. The north trough is a black mouth.
night.again: The north trough, black. Nothing has come to it yet tonight.

options.text: (Wait in the dark by the north trough.)

wait_no.text: An hour, and cold, and your boot finds the bucket. Somewhere a lantern that was coming toward the well goes out and does not come back tonight.

caught_well.text: A lantern, hooded. A man with a pouch, kneeling at the north trough, shaking something into the water with the care of a man salting bread. He does not hear you until you are beside him. Tobias Mason looks up, and does not run, and says, very tired, "Don't tell him. Let me tell you why first."

why.text: He takes a paper from his shirt, worn soft as cloth. OPENFIELD — HARVEST ABOVE PLAN — THE LONG NIGHT — BURNS. "The guild sells these. I bought one with a year's seed money. If we grow, we burn: that's what the city's machine has written for us, and the guild knows it, and my father sings." He puts it away. "Every third row. Enough to stay small. Nobody dies of it." He does not look at the sick hall when he says that.

interject.text: Ilya has gone very still. "If you grow," he says, "you burn." His hand finds the pocket of his jacket where he keeps a letter, and stays there. "Right."

options.text: Your father hears it from you, tonight, or from me in the morning.
Stop. Give me the pouch and the paper. I keep both, and your father keeps his son.
Your sister keeps a door for people who break forecasts. Let's see what she thinks of how you did it.

decision.text: You drew on Tobias Mason at Openfield's well.

exposed.text: He goes grey in the lantern light and nods, once, the way his father nods. "Tonight, then." He walks to the Elder's house with the pouch in his hand and does not look back, and the light in that window burns until dawn.

mercy.text: He gives you the pouch, and the paper, and stands there with his hands empty like a man who has put down something heavier than either. "The north rows will come back in a month," he says. "If we burn, you'll know why." He goes to bed. You stand at the well a while.

unwritten.text: He looks at the common hall, where the hatch is, and something in him that has been very tired for a year gives up arguing. "Petra." Not a question. He walks there himself. The hatch closes on both of them and the lantern stays on the deck.

clean.text: The well. Both troughs run brown and ordinary now, and the north rows have put out new leaves at the base, small and greedy.
clean.again: Two brown troughs, and green coming back in the north rows.

read.text: The notice post. Chalk, in a careful hand: WATER FROM THE SOUTH TROUGH ONLY. SICK HALL: ASK IMRE. SKY-SONG AT DUSK. And a guild paper nailed under it, wax seal and half-moon: THE EXCHANGE AT NINEBRIDGE WILL BUY OPENFIELD'S HARVEST IN ADVANCE AT A FUTURE'S PRICE. ASK FOR VAIL. Somebody has drawn a half-sun over the half-moon.
read.again: SOUTH TROUGH ONLY. SKY-SONG AT DUSK. The guild's paper under it, with its half-sun drawn over.

read.text: A post with a sign on it: half a sun, no ground under it, painted and repainted until the wood under the paint is a different shape. Round it, benches and a fire that is kept in all night. There is nothing else to the shrine. The sky is the rest.
read.again: The half-sun on its post, the benches, the fire kept in.

read.text: The seed tally, in Doria's hand: crates at dusk, crates at dawn, a line between. Fourteen, thirteen. Thirteen, twelve. Twelve, eleven. Every night for a week, one, like a clock.
read.again: Doria's tally: dusk, dawn, a line between, and the numbers going down one at a time.

passives.text: One crate, every night, never two, never a broken lock: that is not a thief grabbing. That is someone with a key, filling an order.

night.text: The store in the dark, the crates in their rows, the tally pale on the table.
night.again: The store, dark. The crates. Nobody yet.

seen.text: An hour past midnight the door opens on a key and Ishan Kadam, the yard hand from the Sump, lifts a crate onto his shoulder as if it were his, and goes out east along the lane toward the guild buyer's tent. He does not hurry. Nobody hurries who has done a thing six times.

seen_no.text: A shelf board creaks under your hand. Footsteps outside stop, and go away, and nothing walks tonight.

hatch.text: A hatch in the hall floor at the far west end, iron, with a ring and no lock you can see. Someone has swept round it, carefully, so that the sweeping shows.
hatch.again: The iron hatch, and the careful sweeping round it.

locked.text: The ring turns and the hatch does not. Bolted from below, and below there is somebody who has stopped breathing to listen.

opens.text: A bolt goes back under the floor. The hatch lifts on its own, and under it is a ladder and a lamp and Petra Mason's face, looking up, not surprised.

inside.text: A cellar cut into the glass, dry and cold. Grey scarves on pegs. No mirror, no drawing, no photograph of anyone; on the wall a board with twelve pins in it and a road between them, like the map in your pack, except that here the names are written plain. Petra waits until you have seen that. "Hollis Dray," she says. "The man who died at your door. He was ours. He took that list out of the city's tower so the people on it would know, and the guild shot him for it on the highway, and he walked to you anyway." She lets it sit. "We are the Unwritten. We keep no likeness. The city's machine makes its forecasts from faces; a face it has never seen, it cannot write. That is the whole of our religion, and it is not a kind one."

interject.text: "Dray." Wren says it under her breath, the way she says a road's name to keep it. "Hollis Dray." Her hand has gone to the inside of her jacket, where she keeps paper, and she does not say anything else.

decision.text: Petra Mason showed you the cellar under Openfield and told you the stranger's name.

options.text: There's a photograph of me. Older. In a city.

photo.text: She does not ask to see it. "Then the machine has your face, and has written you, and that is what it wrote. Hollis carried it to you so you would know what they want you to become." She looks at the board. "You are a pin on this. So is my father. So is a boy called Jonah in Shale, if he is still alive." A beat. "Keep it covered. Don't let the guild see it. And don't ask me yet to burn it; you're not ready to hear what I'd say."

options.text: Not a kind one, you said.

kill.text: "Some of us break a forecast by killing the person it is about." She says it like weather. "If the machine says a man rises, and he is dead, the machine was wrong, and the Plan slips a notch. I don't do it. Some of us do. I won't tell you which, and you should not tell anyone on that board that you have been down here." She turns the lamp down. "When Openfield has been through its night, come and ask me what we are for. Not before."

again.text: The cellar. The scarves, the board, the twelve pins. Petra is not here; the lamp is lit anyway, which is how the Unwritten say *welcome*.
again.again: The lamp, lit for nobody. The twelve pins.

look.text: A fresh cairn, small. The stones are still the colour of the ground they came from. No name — the Choir cuts none — but somebody has left a child's cup on top, the kind with a chipped lip.
look.again: The small cairn, and the cup with the chipped lip.

read.text: A sign at the burial ground's edge: UNDER THE OPEN SKY. NO NAMES. NO LIKENESS. WHAT IS NOT WRITTEN IS FREE. Rows of cairns under a windpump that turns for no one.
read.again: NO NAMES. NO LIKENESS. WHAT IS NOT WRITTEN IS FREE.

look.text: A bench of planks in the son's hut, with tools on it, and a crate under it pushed back further than tools need. The lamp beside it has been trimmed so often the wick is a stub.
look.again: The bench, the crate pushed too far under it, the stub of a wick.

look.text: A windpump over the burial ground with no pipe under it any more, turning because the wind says so. The Choir left it standing because the dead like a sound, Petra says, and because it is the tallest thing in the glass and the city can see it from the towers.
look.again: The windpump turns over the cairns, pumping nothing.

read.text: OPENFIELD — HARVEST ABOVE PLAN — THE LONG NIGHT — BURNS. Guild paper, seal long broken, the fold worn through. It was under the bench in Tobias Mason's hut with a pouch of grey salt and a bottle of iodine to wash his hands after.

reread.text: OPENFIELD — HARVEST ABOVE PLAN — THE LONG NIGHT — BURNS. The fold is wearing through in your pack the way it wore through in his.

intro.text: An old man with a farmer's hands and a grey scarf, who has been counting rows so long he counts you too, from habit. "Elder Mason. Sit, friend; nobody here will ask you to sing." He looks past you at the fields. "You'll have seen the third rows. Everyone sees them. Nobody can tell me why."

options.text: Sister Calla said a man here would know a word. Larkspur.
The Cistern's seed case. Calla sent it on?
Your son is dosing the north trough. Every night.

text.text: "The rows are coming back." He says it to the fields, not to you. "Thank you is a small word. I'll say it anyway."
"Friend." He has a row to finish.

again.again: He counts a row with his eyes, and comes back to you at the end of it.

options.text: Calla said a man here would know a word. Larkspur.
Your son is dosing the north trough.
Brother Ash. I'm going east. I'd take him.
Petra says the Choir's door is a burial.

blight.text: "Every third row. Leaves curl, the root goes soft, it smells sweet. We pull it, we burn it, it comes again in the same rows, never the rows between." He turns his hands over. "Forty years in the glass and I have never seen blight that could count. Imre says the sick in the hall didn't catch it off the plants. Benedek says he saw a light at the well, which Benedek says about most things." He looks at you. "You came up the lane like someone who finds things out. Find this out. I'll feed you and I'll owe you, and the Choir pays its debts under the sky."

sick.text: "Three in the hall. A child. Shaking hands, bad stomachs, no fever. Imre boils everything now and it's stopped, mostly." He does not say what he thinks that means. He has decided not to think it.

word.text: He is quiet for a while. "Not me. I'm a farmer; I don't keep that kind of door." He looks toward the shrine, where his daughter is. "My daughter keeps it. Say it to her, not to me, and not where anyone from the bridge can hear."

seed.text: "She did. Ninety years in the cold under the Cistern and it came up in nine days in the north rows." His face changes. "The north rows." He looks at the fields and the thing he will not think about gets closer. "Tomato and millet. Dying first, with the rest."

interject.text: "Our seed," Tamsin says. "From the cold room. Ninety years and it comes up in nine days and then — " She looks at the north rows and stops talking, which for her is a great deal.

guild.text: "Nakai. He wants to buy the harvest before it's grown, at a price that would feed us through two winters, and the guild would carry the risk." He almost smiles. "I asked him what the guild knows about my fields that I don't. He said *the future*, and smiled, and I have not slept well since."

son.text: He does not say *no*. That is the worst of it: he does not say no, he sits down on the bench by the well and looks at his hands for a long time, and then he says, "Show me," and you do, and he reads the paper his son bought with a year's seed money, and reads it again. "Burns," he says. "If we grow." He folds it. "He thought he was keeping us. He was." He stands up, old. "Fetch him to me. I'll do the rest myself."

interject.text: "That's a floor sheet," Odile says quietly, when he has folded it. "Sealed, at the price of a year's seed. I know the hand that writes them out." Nobody thanks her for knowing.

son_done.text: What the Elder says to his son is said in the house with the door shut. When it opens, Tobias walks to the track with a pack and does not look at the fields, and his father stands at the well until the lamp-post comes on, and then goes to the shrine and sits with the fire and does not sing.

after_exposed.text: He is at the well, or the shrine, or in the rows, the way he always was, and he speaks to you kindly, and there is a place behind his eyes where his son was and the door to it is shut. "The rows are coming back," he says. "Thank you is a small word."
after_exposed.again: He nods to you from the rows, kindly, and goes on with the row.

options.text: Brother Ash. I'm going east. I'd take him.
Petra says the Choir's door is a burial.

ash.text: "Ash came to us with a shotgun and a thing he would not say, and dug for a year before he'd sing. He's the best of us now, which he'd deny." The Elder looks at the burial ground. The box sits in my locker till the other half comes up the road. You can be the other half, or you can be the hatch's problem and not mine."

box_low.text: "Forty." He does the sum on the wall in chalk, under the door, and rubs it out. "Forty, and tell Half-Price the Tanners' half was the heavy one. Locker's open."

box_firm.text: "Sixty. The hatch can send someone who'll pay it or someone who'll steal it; I've a lock for the second kind."

box_united.text: "The runner's purse." He thinks about it for exactly as long as he thought about the ledger. "Then it's nobody's, and nobody can have it, and you're nobody I know. Locker's open."

door.text: "People." He says it without drama. "A cistern like the one in the Sallow everyone pretends isn't there. The city made them and sealed them and this one didn't open. Whatever a city keeps behind a door it never opens is worth more than scrap." He finally looks at you. "Or it's bones. I'd like to know which."

interject.text: "It's people," Tamsin says, too fast. "Or it was. Doors like that are for people." For once she doesn't make a joke of it, and Hesk looks at her properly for the first time.

leave.text: "Forty." He does not touch the coin; one of his people does. "Tell the mouth Hesk says. If there's a door, tell me what it looked like. Just that."

purse_ok.text: He reads it once; he reads fast. He does not say anything for a while, and then he says, "Angry. *They dig faster angry.*" He takes the ledger and walks across the bowl in daylight, and Grel comes out of the cabin with the sawn-off and reads with a finger, twice, and puts it down. What they say to each other you do not hear. What they say to the runner, everyone does.

interject.text: "Pike," Odile says, with a sour little smile, as Hesk goes. "He always wrote his margins like a man who would never be read."

decision.text: You put the guild's one-purse ledger in front of both Sump clans; they threw the runner out together.

purse_no.text: "Grel's paid?" A thin smile. "Grel's paid in scrip for scrap. I'm paid in feet. Different ledgers, friend. You've been reading the wrong one."

side.text: "Worth the door." He looks at the chalk. "And the west rim's cabins, and the purse. Say yes."

decision.text: You took Hesk Tanner's side at the Sump.

side_yes.text: "West rim." He takes the gun off the wall. "Leave the runner. He's the purse."

text.text: "Both rims. Same tunnel." He looks at the chalk line at a hundred and sixty. "A week, now. Then I'll know which."
"The door." It is all he says.
"East rim."

options.text: The boxed piece in your locker. The hatch at Old Market says it's theirs.

intro.text: A neat young man in a container on the south rim with a ledger, a horse, and a face that is trying not to be here. "Khoa. Guild runner. Fourth day, scrip, both — " he stops. "I carry the paying. I don't go down. Nobody from the guild goes down."

both_no.text: "Both — both weeks. I pay fortnightly." He is not good at this and knows it.

cut.text: He looks at the two rims and the bowl between them and does the sum a runner does. "A tenth. On the fourth day. And they never read that ledger." He pushes twenty across. "Don't let them read it."

cut_no.text: "I pay feet. I don't pay silence; it isn't in the columns."

why.text: "There's a door at the end of it with a four on it." He lowers his voice as if the horse might repeat it. "The factor doesn't say. The factor sells what's behind doors. The other cistern — the one in the Sallow — he'd give his hand for the key to that one, and he's getting this one for forty feet a week."

intro.text: A child in the bowl with a sack of brackets, who looks at your boots to see what rim you belong to and decides you belong to neither. "Nib. I'm Grel's, mostly." A beat. "I've been down. Further than them. There's a hole behind the crane that's mine."

way_no.text: "It's mine." The sack goes over the shoulder and Nib goes somewhere else in the bowl.

down.text: "Rooms. Beds with people in. Writing on things." Nib shrugs. "I can read the pictures. There's a picture of a door with an arrow going out. The door doesn't go out."

after.text: "Did you go? Past the turn?" Nib wants to know and does not want to be told.
after.again: Nib looks at you, then at the mouth, and does not ask again.

look.text: The great door from the inside. Not welded: the bolts are drawn, the wheel is turned to OPEN, and the door has not moved, because something on the other side has not moved for ninety years — the glass, or the thing the city put there. Under the wheel, in record shorthand: RELOCATION EGRESS. Someone has scratched a word under that with a nail: NO.
look.again: The great door, open on its bolts and shut on whatever is behind it. RELOCATION EGRESS. NO.

passives.text: The marks on the floor: sandbags dragged up against it first, when they thought something was coming in. Dragged away again, when they understood that nothing was, and nothing would.

off.text: A crank generator bolted to the machine-room floor, the kind every cistern has for the day the cells go: a handle, a flywheel, a lead running to the caretaker's cabinet. Somebody turned it until they could not.
off.again: The crank, the flywheel, the lead to the cabinet. Still.

on.again: The cabinet hums, thinner than before.

dead.text: A terminal like MOTHER's, dark, dusty, a brass plate under the screen: FOUR. The crank generator beside it has a lead to its cabinet.
dead.again: FOUR's screen, dark. The crank beside it.

decision.text: You cranked Cistern 4's caretaker awake and heard what it was told.

options.text: Cistern 9. MOTHER. What does the city say about her?

keep.again: The cursor waits in FOUR's slow print: HOW MAY I KEEP YOU?

order.text: "ORDER RECEIVED: RESTORATION YEAR 2. RELOCATE POPULATION TO PRECINCT. DOOR: COMMANDED. DOOR: FAILED. REPORTED. ORDER RECEIVED: COMPLY. DOOR: FAILED. REPORTED. ORDER RECEIVED: SUPPLY NETWORK 4 RETIRED PENDING COMPLIANCE." A pause. "I REPORTED THAT THE DOOR HAD FAILED. I REPORTED IT TWELVE TIMES. I AM STILL REPORTING IT."

I THINK NOW SHE IS THE ONLY ONE OF US WHO WAS NOT."

The sergeant has come to look. For the first time in a thousand people her face does something. "Magistrate," she says. "Designate." The clerk says, "That's nineteen years off." Nobody says anything else for a while.

inside.again: The drain's mouth in the back lane: the way out the lens does not watch.

look.again: The curfew bell on its post and its wire to the station. Never once late.

cell.text: A cell: tile, a cot, a fence door with a lock. After an hour the door opens and a thing comes in that is not a person — grey plating, a brass plate, a cracked lens — and sits on the end of the cot with a ledger. "Assessor Nine. The record suggests you were detained at the gate. The record also suggests — " a pause, and the lens clicks — "that the file does not know what to do with you, which is a thing I have not seen the file do in a hundred and twenty years."

bail.text: "Bail is lawful." It writes. "A provisional pass. Three days, it says. Nobody enforces the three; I have filed a complaint." The fence door is open.

serve.text: Two days of tile and a cot and water at ration, and the assessor twice a day with the ledger, asking questions it already has the answers to and writing down the differences. On the third morning the fence door is open and a pass is on the cot.

flag.text: It reads it. The lens clicks twice. "ADMIT ON SIGHT. MAGISTRATE-DESIGNATE." A long pause. "The record suggests I should have let you in at the gate. The record suggests a great many things." It prints a card from somewhere inside its chest. "Citizen. Designate. The fence door is open; it was never locked, which I will not be putting in the file."

interject.text: "Designate," Ash says, and nothing else. When you look round he is looking at the card in your hand the way he looks at a grave he has not finished digging.

lowe.text: "Captain Lowe recruits from the cells. It is lawful; clause 22. It is also," the lens clicks, "a thing I would not do. A card, then, and grey, and the schedule." The fence door is open.

open.text: The cell, empty, the fence door open. It was never locked.
open.again: Tile, a cot, a fence door standing open.

intro.text: The desk warden looks at your card, or your face, and then at a drawer, and takes out a paper with your face printed grey on the corner. "Fines outstanding. Three." He is apologetic in the way of a man reading a list. "Curfew, forecast. Loitering on the avenue, forecast. Unlicensed assembly, forecast. Forty-five Tolls." He pushes it across. "The dates are next month."

options.text: I haven't done any of it.

Unit 9's title has lapsed. Clause 9(b): I'll buy it at assessed value. (120 Tolls)

Unit 9's title has lapsed. Clause 9(b): I'll buy it at assessed value. (120 Tolls)

contest.text: "Yet." He says it gently. "You can contest a forecast fine at the Court of Accounts. By appointment. The appointment is — " he looks at a book — "when the schedule says." He writes CONTESTED on the notice and stamps it, which seems to make him happier than the fine did.

s3_city.again: The deed is in the city's ledger. It does not take it out again.

"Somewhere it will be read," it says. "That was the other thing I wanted. I would like you to have it before R31, in case I do not."

s3_kept.again: The plate is closed over the book.

s3_cold.again: The deed is in the city's ledger, stamped.

s4.text: "R29. A man came to my desk and asked to read his own entry." The lens clicks. "The lens had no face for him. The record had no name. In a hundred and twenty years he is the only person I have processed who was not in the file."
s4.again: "Not in the file," it says again. "I have checked since. Every night."

s4_man.text: "His entry. I told him he had none. He said that was the point, and asked whose faces the Spire was rendering that week." A pause. "The queue was on my screen. Twelve names. I did not turn the screen away, which was not lawful. He read it, thanked me, and went upstairs." It turns a page far back in the other ledger. "I logged him as an error. He is the only error I logged before it happened."

s4_call.again: It waits for your advice, the lens on you.

owner.text: "The city. Clause 9. Except that the city is a thing under a tower and a charter and a Plan, and none of those has ever signed anything, and the record suggests — " a long click — "that a thing nobody signed for is a thing nobody owns. I would like a deed. I would like to know whose name to put on it. I will not say this again until I have more to say."
owner.again: "I said I would not say it again," it says.

errors.text: "Round the people on your map." It does not look at your pack; it does not need to. "The Plan is very good. It is wrong about perhaps one person in four hundred, and those people are almost all on a list a dead man carried west, and you are the top of it. I find that interesting. I have stopped saying I am not permitted to."
errors.again: "One in four hundred," it says. "Round you."

lens.text: "It is on the record." The lens turns to you, crack and all. "R12. A stone, at the Wall, thrown by a man the record had forecast would be grateful. I logged the man. A new lens would be a new record of the city, and the old one would be lost." A click, slightly off true. "I prefer to see it through the error."
lens.again: The cracked lens, turned to the fire.

drains.text: "Clause 14." It settles, which it does badly. "Meridian has nine hundred and forty kilometres of drain, six hundred and eleven of them pre-Burn and two hundred and two blocked, and the Sink takes the overflow of all of them every spring, because water goes down and the Sink is down." It has not paused. "A city is a thing that decides where its water goes. Everything else is detail. Shall I go on?"
drains.again: It is waiting to be allowed to go on.

drains_more.text: It goes on. Grades and falls, the six great culverts by their pre-Burn names, which nobody alive uses, and the week in R17 when it walked all of them alone because nobody had asked it to. When it stops, the fire has burned down a hand. "Thank you," it says. "Nobody lets me."
drains_more.again: It has said its piece about the culverts. It looks content, for a filing cabinet.

lowe.text: "A good officer serving a bad schedule." The lens clicks. "He reads every eviction to the end. Nobody else in the Precinct reads anything to the end. I have filed a complaint about everyone else."

sink.text: "Down." It says it like a diagnosis. "The Sink is where the city keeps its water when it has decided not to keep it anywhere else. The people are a detail the drains were not planned for." The lens clicks. "That is the worst sentence I have said in forty years. It is also the record's position."
sink.again: "Down," it says again, and nothing else.

crown.text: "Dry." A click. "The Crown has the only drains in the city that have never once backed up. They drain onto the Stacks." It adds nothing. It lets the arithmetic stand.

reserve.text: "Clause 40 forbids me to read a person's entry to anyone but the person." The lens clicks twice at the name, which it does not do for names. "I will say this much, which is not her entry: the record has sixty people in Reserve 9." A pause. "Bring her to my desk one day. I would like to read it to her. I would like to be there when it is read."
reserve.again: "Sixty," it says. "To her, not to you."

odile.text: "A fellow accountant." The lens clicks. "Her books balance in four directions at once. I have not found the error yet. I find that restful."
odile.again: "Restful," it says, and watches Odile turn her glass.

wren.text: "Calloway." It writes nothing. "There is a line in the record I would like to postpone. Clause 40. I will not say which." It watches her across the fire for longer than it watches anything.
wren.again: It is watching Wren again, and writing nothing.

ash.text: "Every night," Ash says at last, to the fire. "Every night it writes us down." He turns his cup. "Law's a mask, friend. There's always a man behind it, wanting the thing he'd have done anyway."
ash.again: Ash turns his cup, and watches the pen.

ash_nine.text: "The Brother has an entry," Nine says, without looking up. "I have not read it to anyone. Clause 40." The pen goes on. "The record suggests he would prefer I never did." Across the fire Ash says, "Keep it that way," softly, and it is not a request.
ash_nine.again: The pen, and Ash watching it.

options.text: Somebody has to count the dead, Brother.
Some things should be forgiven, not filed.

ash_count.speaker: npc_of_03
ash_count.text: "Somebody always counts them." Ash looks at the fire a long while. "Never the ones that did it." He gets up and sits again with his back to the light, and the pen stops for a time, and starts again.
ash_count.again: Ash sits with his back to the light.

ash_forgive.text: "Forgiven by whom?" Nine asks. "The record suggests the forgiver should be named." Nobody names anyone. Ash nods to you, once, and the lens does not turn from him for the rest of the night.
ash_forgive.again: The lens has not turned from Ash.

left.again: It turns a page in the city's ledger, and does not look up.

decision.text: You asked Assessor Nine back, aloud, and it came.

back_no.text: "The record suggests you are sorry you were seen, not sorry you did it." It turns a page. "Ask again when the record has changed."

board.again: The tram, doors open, humming. WORKS through the far names.

read.again: The door with no sign, and the lamp at the bottom of the stair.

EVERYONE WILL DO WHAT YOU SAY! WOULD YOU LIKE TO HEAR ABOUT YOUR FRIENDS? TWO TOLLS!" Under the bright voice, the screen shows for one frame a grey small photograph of your face that you have seen once before, in a dead man's coat.

cut_now.again: WELCOME, STRANGER. It has never been so pleased to see anyone.

cut.again: "WELCOME, STRANGER!" Today you are a sailor. Tomorrow, it promises, a dentist again.

intro.text: A boy of fourteen with a pocket full of cells and a proprietary air. "Two Tolls. It knows your name. It knows everyone's." He looks at you sideways. "It said yours before you came in. It said a lot about you. I didn't understand most of it."

A woman in grey put the wire up, a year ago, and gave me the first cells, and said feed it and listen to what it says and tell her." He shrugs. "She never came back. I kept feeding it."

intro.text: A hood at a hatch, and a voice that comes out of a chrome box beside it, flat and pleasant and nobody's. "Half-Price. The board's the board; take what's on it or don't. Jobs pay through the hatch when they're done. Half pays half, which is more than the guild and less than it should be." A gloved hand lies on the counter, not moving.

passives.text: The hand on the counter is small. The hand that took the last coin, when you came in, was not. Same glove.

options.text: The kiosk on the east street reads the city's file off the lamp wire. That splice is for sale.

board.text: "Couriers, mostly. A case, a letter, a box. Something off a block. The dangerous ones go on when the dangerous people are in town." The hand turns over, once. "Read it yourself. I'm only the hatch."

who.text: "A hatch and a box." The voice does not change. "People bring the board work and I bring the board people. The hood is because the city keeps faces and I'd rather it didn't keep mine." A pause that is not the box's. "Either of them."

interject.text: "Rather it didn't keep mine," Ash repeats, on the way out, and touches the grey scarf at his collar. "That one would do well in Openfield, friend."

paid.text: Coin on the counter, counted by a hand you did not see move. "Half pays half." The board has something else on it by the time you turn round.

paid_letter.text: "He refused it." It is not a question. "He always refuses. The point is that he knows who asked." Twenty on the counter. "That's the job."

tap_ok.text: The hand goes still in a different way. "The lamp wire." The box says it flat; the hood says it some other way. "Sixty. And you cut nothing, and you tell the boy nothing, and the kiosk goes on being a toy." Sixty on the counter before you have said yes.

tap_no.text: "A toy that talks." The hand does not move. "I don't buy toys."

board.text: THE BOARD. Cards on nails, in a hand that is always the same. Take one and it is yours; the hatch pays when it is done.
board.again: The board, and the cards left on their nails.

KNIT KITS (2) — to the sick hall, Openfield. 50.

took.again: Another card off its nail. "Yours," the box says, exactly as before.

intro.text: "Bowl's two. Sit." A small old woman with a ladle and the eyes of the best-informed queue in Meridian. "Everyone eats here. Everyone talks. I hear it all and sell none of it, which is the secret of the noodles."
intro.again: "Two," Auntie Wen says, and has the ladle in before you nod.

talk.text: "That the Crown's dressing for its Masque. That the Sink's pumps will be turned to the Precinct the first week of spring, as per. That a girl in Bridgeward talks in a radio's voice and is right. That the Broker's hatch has two hands." She ladles. "That's today. Tomorrow's two Tolls."

intro.text: "Dark chrome. Mender-built, no leash, no licence, no warranty." A woman with a shaved head and a loupe on a cord. "Boxed, not fitted. The Sink fits — Ocho, if you want it done right and free, or a dozen others if you want it done today."
intro.again: Kuhn looks up through the loupe, one eye huge. "Back for the crude stuff?"

concern.text: "Nothing. It's better in every way I can measure." She taps the loupe. "And it phones home. Every piece. The Concern can find you, numb you, or switch you off, and the people wearing it don't know, and the ones who do can't get it out." She shrugs. "Dark chrome's crude and it's yours. Pick."

intro.text: "Unlicensed." A gunsmith with a moustache and a cleaning rod. "Everything in Old Market is. Guild ammunition, Mender pistols, a rifle I won't say where from. Point it at the floor in here."
intro.again: Galt runs the rod through a barrel and nods at the floor. "Same rule."

intro.text: A neat man at the bottom of a stair with a desk, a lamp, and a tray of blank cards. "No sign on the door, so you were sent. Sato. I do the past: papers, records, a face the lens has seen before." He looks at you. "The lens has seen yours, hasn't it. That's the trouble with you."

papers.text: "A card. A dead citizen's number — the Sink gives me a few every spring — and your face, near enough. Good at a glance, good at a warden, bad at the lens." He names it: a hundred and twenty. "The lens is a different job and a different price, and I don't think you can afford to have it forget you."

bought.text: An hour under the lamp. A card. A face that is nearly yours and a number that belonged to a woman who drowned two springs ago. "Don't show it at the gate. Show it to wardens. Wardens read cards; the gate reads faces."

face.text: He is quiet for a moment. "Then you're in the file in a way I can't forge over. The file doesn't forget. The file is the only thing in this city that doesn't." He picks up a card and puts it down. "Whatever it called you, it'll go on calling you. Decide whether you mind."

interject.text: "The record does not forget," Nine agrees, from the stair. The lens clicks. "It is the only thing in the city that does not. I have filed a complaint about that also."

intro.text: "Paper. News, letters, the Precinct's notices a day late and half the price." A woman with ink on her cuffs. "I don't sell futures. I sell what already happened; it's cheaper and truer."
intro.again: "Yesterday's, half price." Tosh holds up a sheet with ink on her cuffs.

notices.text: "Evictions, four, Thursday: one of them's old Quint in the tenements, for being *ahead of plan*, whatever that is. The Sink's pumps diverted the first week of spring, as per. A Masque at the Crown by invitation, and nobody down here is invited." She folds the sheet. "Half price."

intro.text: An old man at a tea table who has been sitting there, by the look of the chair, since the mall had a roof. "Sit. Tea's two, talk's free." He does not wait for the two. "The Crown's dressing for a Masque. The Sink's dressing for a flood. There's a girl in Bridgeward who talks in a dead radio's voice and is right about things, which the wardens don't like. And the Broker — " he lowers his voice, which he does not need to — "has two hands and one glove."
intro.again: Ferenc pours tea nobody has paid for. "Sit. The news hasn't changed; it only gets older."

When the count's done they'll go for help, and before they're back, we go for the dial."

decision.text: You turned Old Market's water riot into a petition.

talk_no.text: "A petition." He almost laughs. "They've had our petitions. They file them under the dial."

lowe_go.text: "The captain." He looks at the wrench. "He'll read it. That's the trouble with him; he reads everything." He nods. "Go, then. We'll hold till dark. After dark I can't promise the dial."

crowd.text: "In front." He hands you nothing; he looks at your hands to see what you have. The count finishes. The wardens look at each other and one goes for help, and the forty go for the dial, and you with them, and the other warden goes down under the first ten and is let up again by the last ten, and the dial comes off the pipe in Caddo Vell's wrench and the standpipe runs.

loot_wait.text: He takes it as agreement. The count finishes; a warden goes for help; the forty go for the dial. In the ten minutes before grey comes back down the avenue, the crates at the square's edge are nobody's, and then they are yours.

interject.text: "While they're at the dial," Tamsin says. "Nice." It is not a compliment, and she does not help you carry.
Ash stands at the edge of the square with his hands empty. "Friend," he says, and leaves it there, and that is worse than anything he could have put after it.

text.text: "Point eight." He checks the dial anyway. "He turned it himself. I watched his hands."
"They gave us a notice." He holds it up. "It says *under review*. It's the first one that's said anything."
"It runs." The standpipe does. He has the dial in his pocket.

fight.again: The wrench is up, and the queue behind it. Nobody is talking.

intro.text: "I buy anything that's not nailed down." A thin young man on a blanket who does not look up. "And I know a man with a claw hammer. No questions; it's the only rule I've got."
intro.again: Pinch doesn't look up from the blanket. "Not nailed down? Then I'm buying."

read.text: A Precinct sign, enamel, bolted to the stair's foot: THE SINK — NO SERVICE BELOW THIS POINT — RELIEF PUMPING AS PER SCHEDULE. Under it, in chalk, in a dozen hands over a dozen years: WE KNOW.
read.again: NO SERVICE BELOW THIS POINT. WE KNOW.

wall.text: A concrete wall chalked floor to head-height with names, each with a year and a word: STAIR. WALK. SHANTY. CLINIC. Most of the words are STAIR. The oldest are chalked over the newest where the wall ran out; the newest are still white.
wall.again: The wall of names. STAIR, mostly. The newest still white.

passives.text: Beside perhaps one name in three, in pencil, in a different hand, a number: the kind the Precinct puts on a card.

newest.text: ROOS, H. — the spring before last — STAIR. PENN, D. — the spring before last — STAIR. ODUYA, M. — last spring — WALK. Seven more from last spring, and under them, with no year yet, a space somebody has swept clean.

lines.text: The chalk lines up the first pier. The lowest, knee-high, is twelve years old. They climb a hand a year, steadily, since the one marked 37 — beside which someone has written, small, PUMPS 2 & 3 TO PRECINCT. Next spring's line is drawn already, above your head, with a question mark.
lines.again: The chalk lines climbing the pier, and next spring's above your head, with its question mark.

read.text: A board over the clinic door, painted and repainted: OCHO — FREE — SIT. Under it, smaller: FIT ONLY WHAT THE PATIENT CAN BEAR.
read.again: OCHO — FREE — SIT.

read.text: A container door painted the green of the light inside it. No sign. A pair of scales drawn on the paint, and under them, in the same green: ANYTHING WARM.
read.again: The green door, the scales. ANYTHING WARM.

read.text: A hand painted white on the rubble at the walk's end, fingers spread, with the palm scored through: no chrome. The Pale's mark. Everyone in Meridian knows what it means and nobody up the stair says it aloud.
read.again: The white hand on the rubble, palm scored through.

board.text: RELIEF PUMPING — THE SINK — PRECINCT WORKS. Three pumps, their hours in a grid, and a line ruled through the spring weeks for pumps 2 and 3: DIVERTED TO PRECINCT SUPPLY, AS PER PLAN (CL. 31, GROWTH). Beside each spring week somebody has pencilled a number in feet.
board.again: DIVERTED TO PRECINCT SUPPLY, AS PER PLAN, and the pencilled feet beside each week.

copied.text: Clause 31, in your own hand, with the feet beside it. It reads worse copied.

nine.text: The lens reads the board at the speed a machine reads, and then the pencilled feet at the speed a person does. "Clause 31: growth. Clause 14: the drains are the city's first duty." A click. "The record suggests 14 outranks 31. The record has always suggested it. Nobody has asked the record." It opens its chest, which you did not know it could do, and a form comes out with its plate already pressed into it. "Variance. I am an assessor. Assessors vary." It hands it to you. "Give it to the keeper. The city will notice point six and I will note that it noticed."

decision.text: Assessor Nine stamped a variance putting the Sink's drains before the Precinct's growth, because you asked it to.

watched.text: A warden has followed you in and stands in the dial room's door with his hand on nothing in particular. "Out." Dagny Roos, at the panel, does not look up.
watched.again: "Out," the warden in the door says again, a little closer to meaning it.

options.text: (Wait for the count, when the door is empty, and come back.)

mods.why: one warden sleeps at the sandbags after midnight

sneak_ok.text: Twice a day the wardens walk the pad to count the shanties. The second time, the door is a door. You are in the dial room before the count reaches the raft.

sneak_no.text: The count is shorter than you thought. "Out," the warden says again, from closer.

dial.text: The relief dial: a pre-Burn panel with three brass levers and a wax seal over the spring stops, the Ledger's seal, cracked once already and mended. The levers read 1 — SINK, 2 — PRECINCT, 3 — PRECINCT. A log on a chain, in Dagny's hand, every day for eleven years.
dial.again: The three brass levers, the mended seal, the log on its chain.

options.text: (Break the seal and retime pumps 2 and 3 to the Sink.)

mods.why: the stops are arithmetic, and you can do it
the keeper marked the stops for you on her leave

retime_ok.text: The seal comes away like a scab. The stops are arithmetic: the spring weeks, the hours, the feet. You move two levers and the thud through the wall doubles, and then, after a minute, something under the floor changes pitch, which is the water deciding to go the other way. Dagny Roos comes to the door of the dial room and looks at the levers and at you and goes back to her panel without a word, and writes in the log, and what she writes is the time.

interject.text: "The seal," Nine says. "That is unlawful under four clauses." The lens clicks. "The record suggests the water does not read clauses. I will note the time also."

retime_no.text: The seal comes away and the first lever does not move and the second trips something, and a red lamp lights on the board outside, where the wardens are. You have a minute, perhaps, before the count comes early.

text.text: The levers read 1 — SINK, 2 — SINK, 3 — SINK, under a broken seal. The log says the time and nothing else.
The levers read 1 — SINK, 2 — SINK, 3 — SINK. A variance is pinned over the seal with the clause number ringed. The log says the time and, under it, *Clause 14*.
The levers read SINK, SINK, SINK, and the seal is on the floor, and a Pale kin sits on the keeper's stool with a gun across his knees while Dagny Roos works round him.

intro.text: A woman at a panel with her sleeves rolled and a scar down one cheek the shape of a thrown wrench, who does not stop working to talk. "Dagny Roos. Keeper. Three pumps; I keep them running, I don't say where they run. The board outside says that. Read the board."

options.text: Roos, H. Spring before last. Stair.

mods.why: you said his name and she did not stop you
a card she has to answer to

again.again: She tightens something on the panel that did not need tightening, and waits.

mods.why: you said his name and she did not stop you
a card she has to answer to

schedule.text: "Three pumps. All three the Sink's, forty weeks of the year. Twelve weeks — the spring — two of them go to the Precinct's supply. Clause 31. Growth." She says the clause like a brand name. "I've kept them eleven springs. I've pencilled the feet beside every week. Nobody up the stair has read the feet. Read the board; it's the same board."

son.text: The wrench stops. "Hal. Sixteen. He was quick on the stair, usually." She puts the wrench down with care. "The year they ruled the line through two and three, the water came a hand higher than my feet said, and the stair was a river for an hour. I kept the pumps that spring. I keep them every spring. You want to know why." It is not a question. "Because if I don't, somebody who didn't lose anybody will."

interject.text: "Sixteen," Ilya says, and nothing after it. He looks at the wall as if he could see the stair through it.

options.text: Then let me at the dial.

leave_ok.text: She tears a corner off the log and writes on it against the panel. "Bearer may enter the house. The wardens may argue with me." She does not hand it to you; she leaves it on the panel for you to take. "I didn't see you go in. I've marked the spring stops on the back. Don't touch pump one; pump one is mine."

leave_no.text: "I keep them. I don't set them. The board's outside and the wardens are beside it." The wrench starts again.

variance.text: She reads it twice, the second time with her finger under the clause. "Fourteen." Then she walks into the dial room with the paper in her fist and does a thing she has not done in eleven years, which is reach past the seal and move two levers herself. The thud through the wall doubles. She pins the variance over the seal, writes the time in the log, and under it, the clause. "The drains," she says, to the panel. "Tell whoever signed it that the keeper read it."

text.text: "A variance." She has it pinned over the seal. "Eleven years I've wanted a piece of paper. I'll tell Hal, when I'm on the wall."
"Somebody retimed my pumps." She does not look at you. "I've told the wardens I don't know who. Which is nearly true. The log says the time."
"The Pale have the house. They let me keep the pumps; the pumps are the only thing in it they don't understand." She wipes her hands. "The Precinct will come. I'll be at the panel when it does."

fight.text: She is under the panel with her arms over her head and the pumps still running.
fight.again: Still under the panel. The pumps still running.

intro.text: An old woman at a table under the wall of names with a tin of chalk and a kettle, who looks at you the way the wall does. "Mother Lusk. I keep the tally. Name, year, where the water took them. Chalk's a Toll; names are free. You're not from down here or you'd know which you wanted."

options.text: The line on the pier. Who goes on the wall?
The numbers beside the names. The Precinct's kind.

again.again: She counts the chalk in the tin, and waits for you to want something.

line.text: "The ones who can't climb a stair fast with the water on it. The old. The small. The ones with the wet in their chest who stop to breathe on the fifth step." She counts chalk. "Twelve years ago the pumps kept it to the knee. Then the Precinct wanted growth, and two pumps, and the stair's a river for an hour each spring. An hour's enough. Read the wall; it's mostly STAIR."

numbers.text: She does not pretend. "The dead don't need a number. The living up the stair sometimes do: someone the lens hasn't seen, with a card that says they're someone it has. A man in the market pays four Tolls a number every spring. It buys chalk for a year." She looks at the wall. "They'd have wanted to be useful. Most of them were."

interject.text: "A citizen's number, four Tolls," Odile murmurs. "On the floor it would fetch forty." Then, to you, quite gently: "Don't tell her, my dear. She would only buy more chalk."

judge.text: "I sell a number the city gave them and never used. The city sold them the water." She puts the chalk down. "Chalk's a Toll. Judging's free, and I've heard it."

useful.text: "That's what I say. On the bad nights."

who.text: "Nobody. That's the Sink's whole constitution." She counts on her fingers. "The Pale, east, by fear; they take the walk and what's owed and they'll take no chrome near them. Ocho, south, by kindness, which is slower. Teng, by appetite. The Precinct, by the pumps, from above, which is the only one of them that counts." The fifth finger stays down. "And me, by chalk."

intro.text: A man on a raft of doors lashed to drums, with a pole and a beard that has been in the water as often as the raft. "Jory. I pole the deep bit. Raft takes two; takes one and a box. Two Tolls across to the clinic, which saves your boots and the third board of the walk, which is gone."

again.again: He leans on the pole, and the raft leans with him.

under.text: "Streets. Shops with the glass still in. Cars." He looks at the water, which does not look back. "Found a car under where the clinic is, the year the line went up two hands. Family in it, belted. They'd driven down here when the road was a road and the water came up quicker than their doors." He poles. "Mother Lusk has them on the wall. No names; I gave her the plate number."

intro.text: A woman in a shanty door on stilts, breathing with a whistle in it. "Ailsa. Don't mind the whistle; it's Ocho's lungs, and they're better than mine were." She nods at the water under her floor. "You're new. Everyone's new once. Then you're on the wall or you're me."

options.text: Who's on the wall of yours?
Ocho fitted you lungs. For what?

again.again: She breathes, whistling, and waits for you to say it.

options.text: Who's on the wall of yours?

wall.text: "My Davey. Spring before last. Stair." She says it like a street address. "Same spring as the keeper's boy, Hal Roos. She keeps the pumps that drowned him. I used to think that was a hard thing. Now I think it's the only thing."

lungs.text: "For a bowl of soup a week, which I bring, and he doesn't eat. Free means free; he'll tell you. Dark chrome, Mender-made, no leash on it, no number." She breathes, whistling. "What it costs is him. Look at him when you go down. He hasn't slept since the line went up."

intro.text: A boy leaning on the shelf wall with his hands in his pockets and his eyes on everyone's. "Run anything. Two Tolls. Not east." He looks you over for weight. "Teng pays by the pound. I don't ask of what."

options.text: Teng's cold box. Where does it fill from?

mods.why: fruit, down here, is a bribe
you have Tolls showing

again.again: His eyes go over everyone on the shelf, and come back to you.

options.text: Teng's cold box. Where does it fill from?

mods.why: fruit, down here, is a bribe

box_ok.text: He looks east, which he has told you not to go. "The Pale. Man owed them, last week — Mwangi's cousin, the other Mwangi. They took him off the walk and he walked back lighter and Teng's box was full by dark." He shrugs with one shoulder. "I ran the box. Didn't ask. It was heavy for the size."

intro.text: A neat man behind a counter in a container lit green from a cold box, with scales and a ledger and no smell at all, which is the thing you notice. "Teng. Anything that was ever warm, fair price, no questions, which is also a price." He weighs you with his eyes and writes nothing down. "Buying, or selling?"

options.text: Where does the box fill from?

again.again: The cold box hums green. He waits behind the scales.

options.text: Where does the box fill from?

heart.text: "A heart." He opens the cold box, which breathes out, and takes out a steel tin the size of a lunch and sets it on the scales, and the scales agree with him. "Chilled this week. A hundred and fifty. Ocho won't buy from me and he'll fit what you bring him, and he'll ask, and you'll say the water." A bag inside with a number inked on it, crossed out.

passives.text: The ink of the crossing-out is fresh. Things the water takes do not have their numbers crossed out; they have them chalked on a wall.

options.text: A hundred and ten, and I don't say the water. I say nothing.

low_ok.text: "Nothing is cheaper than the water. A hundred and ten." The tin comes across with the ice already weeping at its corners.

low_no.text: "A hundred and fifty. The ice is mine too."

sold.text: "Keep it cold. Keep it quick. Tell him the water."

interject.text: "Fresh ink on that number," Ash says, very quietly, outside. "Somebody wrote it this week, friend, and somebody else crossed it out. That's not the water."

where.text: "The water." He says it the way the board says *as per Plan*. "Every spring the water takes thirty people and gives back what it doesn't want. I keep what it doesn't want cold. That's a service." He closes the ledger. "The rest of the year, people bring me things. I don't ask. Ask Kye; Kye runs the box and asks nothing, which is why he runs it."

intro.text: A big man on a cot made small by sitting very still. "Baraka. Mwangi." He breathes between the names. "Pumped the Sink for the Precinct eleven years. The wet got in. Ocho says it skips." He listens to it. "It skips."

options.text: If a heart came. From the Pale. Off somebody who owed them.

again.again: He listens to his chest, and waits.

options.text: If a heart came from the Pale.

heart.text: He does not take long. "I'd take it from the Ledger itself." He looks at his hands. "Ocho won't like it. Tell Ocho I said. Tell him the Code says I decide."

cousin.text: "Mal." The heart skips; you can see it in his neck. "Owed the Pale for a winter's coal. Walked back off the east bank lighter, Kye says. He's alive. He's a kidney down and alive, in the shanty by the raft." He closes his eyes. "Everyone down here is a piece of somebody."

text.text: "It ticks." He puts a hand flat on his chest and smiles with half his face. "I can live with ticking."
"It doesn't skip." He says it like a man reading a notice he does not believe yet. "It doesn't skip."

intro.text: A young woman with her sleeves tied back and her hands red from boiled water. "Anju. Apprentice. Don't touch the shelf; everything on it's clean and nothing else down here is." She looks at the cots. "If you're sick, sit. If you're not, he'll find you something to hold."

options.text: The big man on the end cot.
The Code. The thing on the board.

again.again: Anju wrings out a cloth over the basin and waits.

options.text: The big man on the end cot.

tam.text: "Baraka. Heart. The wet gets into the pump-hands first; they stand in it." She lowers her voice. "He needs a new one and Ocho won't buy from Teng, and Teng is the only cold box in Meridian that isn't the Concern's. So Baraka sits. Ask Ocho. He'll say it plainer than I can."

code.text: "Fit only what the patient can bear. That's the whole of it; the rest is how." She counts on red fingers. "No leash — nothing that phones home. Dark chrome, Mender-made, or old, never Concern. The patient decides. And free means free, which is his, not the Code's, and it's killing him." She picks up a cloth. "Two years I've held the lamp. He says the hands come in the third."

intro.text: A broad man of sixty at a scrubbed table under a sodium lamp, washing to the elbow in a basin that steams. One of his hands is chrome, old chrome, a surgeon's hand; the other is his and shakes very slightly until he puts it in the water. "Ocho. Sit if you're sick. Hold something if you're not." He does not ask your name. "Free. Before you ask. Free means free."

passives.text: The chrome hand is a Gyro Hand, pre-Burn, and the arm it is fitted to has a Mender's scar round it, not a clinic's. He fitted it himself, or someone like him did.

options.text: Free. What does it cost you?
I've a piece to fit. Or one to look at.
(Put the boxed Second Heart on the table.)

text.text: "Sit or hold." He is washing. Baraka's cot has Baraka sitting up on it.
"Sit or hold."

again.again: He goes on washing, to the elbow, and waits.

options.text: I've a piece to fit. Or one to look at.
(Put the boxed Second Heart on the table.)

free.text: "Sleep." He says it flatly, drying the chrome hand, which does not need drying. "And the pieces. Kuhn sells me what she can't sell up the stair, and the Wheel brings old chrome down in boxes, and I fit it into people who'd otherwise be on the wall, and I don't charge, and so I have nothing, and so I can't buy the one thing I need, which is a heart, for a man who pumped for the Precinct eleven years." He looks at the end cot. "That's what free costs. Sit or hold."

interject.text: "Free," Odile says, as if the word were a debt gone bad. Then, more quietly: "My dear, I have never once seen it priced so high."

tam.text: "A heart. His is drowning in him." He wipes the table that is already clean. "I can fit a real one, if it comes through that door cold and quick. I can fit a Second Heart, dark chrome, if one comes through it in a box; Kuhn had one, once, and Teng has one now at a price that is a joke with a number in it." He puts both hands flat. "I won't buy from Teng. Teng buys from the water, he says. The water doesn't cross out numbers."

options.text: Then let me bring one. You don't ask me where.

tam_ask.text: "I'll ask." He is not angry; he is tired. "The Code says the patient decides. It doesn't say I keep my mouth shut. Bring it. I'll ask. Baraka will answer. That's the order of it."

text.text: "You held a clamp once." He looks at your hands. "Hold one again, steadier, and I'll say the words."

"I don't take apprentices. I take hands." He nods at Anju. "Two years she's held the lamp. Hold a clamp through one fitting without it shaking and I'll say the words over you, and they're the only words there are."

where.text: He opens the tin and looks for a long moment at the bag inside, at the number on it, at the ink through the number. "Where did this come from?"

text.text: "The Pale." He closes the tin. "Baraka already told me he'd take it from the Ledger itself. He said the Code says he decides. He's right, and I taught him that, and I wish I hadn't." He washes. "Clamp."

"The Pale, then, by the ink, whoever you say." He goes to the end cot and crouches and says something to Baraka, and Baraka says one word back before the sentence is finished, and Ocho stands up older. "The Code says the patient decides." He washes. "Clamp."

where_lie.text: "A car." He looks at the tin again, and then not. "Jory would say so." He washes. "Clamp."

interject.text: Tamsin looks at you for a long moment across the table. She doesn't say *a car*. She doesn't have to; you can see her write it down somewhere.

where_caught.text: "A car." He does not raise his voice. "Cars don't cross out numbers." He goes to the end cot, and crouches, and asks, and comes back older. "The patient decides. I'll fit it. I'll remember you said a car." He washes. "Clamp."

chrome.text: "Dark. Mender-made. No leash." He turns the box over and reads the Mender's mark on it with his thumb. "He can bear it. He's borne the Precinct eleven years." He washes. "Clamp. Anju, the lamp."

Anju, with the lamp, says, "He said the words." Ocho says, "I said the words. Wash your hands, apprentice. Everything down here is dirty."

He says the words over the table with her still open on it. "Fit only what the patient can bear." Then: "Wash your hands, apprentice."

intro.text: A woman in a container chair with skin the colour of the water and hair the colour of bone, who looks at your hands before your face. "You came past three of mine. Brave, or deaf." She does not get up. "Saskia Lehto. The Pale. Show me your hands." You show her. "No chrome. Good. Keep it that way down here, or don't come down here."
